# The Momentum Effect {#sec-momentum-replication}

Do stocks that recently outperformed continue to outperform?
Following Chapter 11 of @bali2016, we compare seven measures of prior returns and examine how their predictive power changes with the return horizon.
@jegadeeshTitman1993 document that portfolios buying recent winners and selling recent losers earn positive returns over several months.

## Measuring Momentum

At the end of month $t$, the main measure compounds returns from $t-11$ through $t-1$.
Skipping month $t$ separates the signal from the most recent return, which is used to measure short-term reversal.

$$
\operatorname{Mom}_{i,t}
=100\left[\prod_{m=t-11}^{t-1}(1+R_{i,m})-1\right].
$$ {#eq-bem11-momentum}

In BEM's Equation (11.1), $R_{i,m}$ is the stock's monthly return in decimal form and $\operatorname{Mom}_{i,t}$ is measured in percentage points.
We compound the available returns and require at least nine observations.
For the lagged 12- and six-month alternatives, the minimum counts are ten and five.
For the 12-, nine-, six-, and three-month windows that include month $t$, the minimum counts are ten, seven, five, and three, respectively.

```{python}
import polars as pl

from eap_pl import build_book_to_market, build_momentum, build_sizes, monthly_panel

first = pl.date(1963, 6, 1)
last = pl.date(2012, 11, 1)
keys = ["permno", "month"]
signals = {
    "mom": "`mom`", "lag12": "Rₜ₋₁₂:ₜ₋₁", "lag6": "Rₜ₋₆:ₜ₋₁",
    "r12m": "`r12m`", "r9m": "`r9m`", "r6m": "`r6m`", "r3m": "`r3m`",
}

sizes = build_sizes()
book_to_market = build_book_to_market(sizes).select(*keys, "bm")
panel = (
    monthly_panel(sizes, first, last)
    .join(build_momentum(first, last), on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
    .join(book_to_market, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
)
```

The formation sample runs from June 1963 through November 2012.
The panel uses the beta, size, and positive book-to-market measures from @sec-bem-beta, @sec-size-replication, and @sec-value-replication.
Holding-month excess returns use the delisting treatment in @sec-bem-returns.

## Correlations

Calculate cross-sectional correlations in each formation month and average them over time.
The Pearson correlations use 0.5% winsorization in each tail of the paired observations.
The Spearman correlations use the original ranks.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem11-correlations
#| tbl-cap: Correlations of momentum with beta, size, and book-to-market (BEM Table 11.2)

from eap_pl import period_correlations

controls = {"beta": "Beta", "log_cap": "Size", "bm": "`bm`"}
correlations = (
    period_correlations(panel, [*controls, *signals], "month")
    .select(pl.exclude("month").mean())
    .row(0, named=True)
)

show_table(pl.DataFrame([
    {
        "Method": method, "Characteristic": label,
        **{name: correlations[f"{method} {control}–{signal}"]
           for signal, name in signals.items()},
    }
    for method in ("Pearson", "Spearman")
    for control, label in controls.items()
]))
```

`mom` is more strongly correlated with size than with beta or book-to-market.

## Momentum and Stock Returns

### Univariate Portfolio Analysis

Each month, sort the stocks with a valid signal into ten portfolios using breakpoints from all stocks with that signal.
Value weights use market capitalization at formation.
Returns and alphas are in percentage points per month.
For each winner-minus-loser spread, regress the monthly return series on an intercept, on the market factor, or on the three Fama–French factors to estimate its mean, CAPM alpha, or FF alpha.
Parentheses report six-lag Newey–West $t$-statistics [@neweywest1987].

```{python}
from era_pl import load_parquet
from eap_pl import format_fit, hac
from eap_pl._portfolios import assign_portfolio, portfolio_months, spread

factors = (
    load_parquet("factors_monthly", "ff")
    .select(
        month=pl.col("date").dt.month_start(),
        market=100 * pl.col("mktrf"),
        smb=100 * pl.col("smb"),
        hml=100 * pl.col("hml"),
        rf=100 * pl.col("rf"),
    )
    .collect()
)
ff3 = ["market", "smb", "hml"]
weights = {"VW": "Value weighted", "EW": "Equal weighted"}


def spread_statistics(series, weight, *, ff_factors=ff3, capm=True):
    sample = (series.select("month", weight)
              .join(factors, on="month", validate="m:1").sort("month"))
    models = {"Return": "1"}
    if capm:
        models["CAPM α"] = "market"
    models["FF α"] = " + ".join(ff_factors)
    return {
        name: format_fit(hac(f"{weight} ~ {rhs}", sample), "Intercept")
        for name, rhs in models.items()
    }
```

```{python}
deciles = {str(i): i for i in range(1, 11)}
formation = panel.select(*keys, "cap", *signals)
members = {
    signal: assign_portfolio(
        formation.select(*keys, "cap", signal).filter(pl.col(signal).is_finite()),
        signal, 10, "month",
    ).drop(signal)
    for signal in signals
}

one_month = panel.select(*keys, "market", "excess")
decile_returns = {
    signal: portfolio_months(
        stocks.join(one_month, on=keys, validate="1:1")
        .with_columns(pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("1mo")),
        ["portfolio"],
    )
    for signal, stocks in members.items()
}
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem11-deciles
#| tbl-cap: Momentum-sorted decile portfolios (BEM Table 11.3)
#| tbl-subcap:
#|   - Momentum-sorted portfolio characteristics
#|   - Portfolio returns and winner-minus-loser spreads
#| echo: false

characteristics = {"mom": "`mom`", "beta": "Beta", "cap": "Market cap (millions)", "bm": "`bm`"}
mom_groups = (
    members["mom"].drop("cap")
    .join(panel.select(*keys, *characteristics), on=keys, validate="1:1")
    .group_by("month", "portfolio").agg(pl.col(*characteristics).mean())
    .group_by("portfolio").agg(pl.col(*characteristics).mean())
    .sort("portfolio")
)
show_table(pl.DataFrame([
    {"Characteristic": label, **dict(zip(deciles, mom_groups[column]))}
    for column, label in characteristics.items()
]))

decile_rows = []
for weight, label in weights.items():
    for signal, name in signals.items():
        monthly = decile_returns[signal]
        means = monthly.group_by("portfolio").agg(pl.col(weight).mean()).sort("portfolio")
        stats = spread_statistics(spread(monthly, 10, 1, "portfolio", weight), weight)
        decile_rows.append({
            "Weights": label, "Signal": name, **dict(zip(deciles, means[weight])),
            "10–1": stats["Return"], "CAPM α": stats["CAPM α"], "FF α": stats["FF α"],
        })
show_table(pl.DataFrame(decile_rows))
```

The `mom` winner-minus-loser spread averages 1.94% per month with value weights and 1.14% with equal weights.

### Returns at Longer Horizons

Keep the formation-month decile assignments and capitalization weights.
For each $k$, attach the return in month $t+k$ and compute the spread across stocks with a return in that month.
A delisting contributes its adjusted return in the month it occurs.
We use realized returns through December 2012 and match the factors to the month in which each return is realized.

```{python}
from eap_pl._data import monthly_stock_returns

holding_returns = (
    monthly_stock_returns(first.dt.offset_by("1mo"), last.dt.offset_by("1mo"))
    .collect()
    .join(factors.select("month", "rf", "market"), on="month", validate="m:1")
    .select("permno", "market", holding="month", excess=100 * pl.col("ret") - pl.col("rf"))
)


def returns_at_horizon(stocks, k):
    realized = (
        stocks.with_columns(holding=pl.col("month").dt.offset_by(f"{k}mo"))
        .drop("month")
        .join(holding_returns, on=["permno", "holding"], validate="1:1")
        .rename({"holding": "month"})
    )
    return portfolio_months(realized, ["portfolio"])
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem11-horizons
#| tbl-cap: Winner-minus-loser returns and FF alphas by horizon (BEM Table 11.4)
#| echo: false

horizon_results = {}
for signal, stocks in members.items():
    extremes = stocks.filter(pl.col("portfolio").is_in([1, 10]))
    for k in range(1, 13):
        monthly = decile_returns[signal] if k == 1 else returns_at_horizon(extremes, k)
        for weight in weights:
            high_minus_low = spread(monthly, 10, 1, "portfolio", weight)
            horizon_results[signal, weight, k] = spread_statistics(
                high_minus_low, weight, capm=False,
            )

show_table(pl.DataFrame([
    {
        "Weights": label, "Signal": name, "Statistic": metric,
        **{f"t+{k}": horizon_results[signal, weight, k][metric] for k in range(1, 13)},
    }
    for weight, label in weights.items()
    for signal, name in signals.items()
    for metric in ("Return", "FF α")
]))
```

The value-weighted `mom` spread turns negative at the longer horizons, reaching −0.63% in month $t+12$.
Its FF alpha in that month is close to zero.

### Controlling for Market Capitalization

First divide stocks into five capitalization groups.
Then compute `mom` quintile breakpoints separately within each capitalization group.
The last column averages the control portfolios each month before calculating the mean return or estimating an alpha.

```{python}
from eap_pl import bivariate_months

sort_panel = panel.select(*keys, "mom", "beta", "cap", "bm", "excess", "market")


def two_way_results(
    monthly, weight, control_labels, *, ff_factors=ff3, show_cells=False, show_average=True,
):
    groups = monthly.partition_by("control", as_dict=True)
    series = {label: groups[i,] for i, label in enumerate(control_labels, 1)}
    if show_average:
        series["Average"] = monthly.group_by("month", "target").agg(
            pl.col(weight).mean(), pl.col("market").first(),
        )

    rows = []
    if show_cells:
        for target in range(1, 6):
            rows.append({
                "Statistic": f"`mom` {target}",
                **{label: f'{cell.filter(pl.col("target") == target)[weight].mean():.2f}'
                   for label, cell in series.items()},
            })

    stats = {
        label: spread_statistics(
            spread(cell, 5, 1, "target", weight).with_columns(
                pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("1mo")
            ),
            weight, ff_factors=ff_factors,
        )
        for label, cell in series.items()
    }
    rows.extend({
        "Statistic": f"5–1 {metric}",
        **{label: value[metric] for label, value in stats.items()},
    } for metric in ("Return", "CAPM α", "FF α"))
    return [{"Weights": weights[weight], **row} for row in rows]


quintiles = [str(i) for i in range(1, 6)]
size_momentum = bivariate_months(sort_panel, "cap", "mom", nyse=False, dependent=True)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem11-size
#| tbl-cap: Dependent sorts on capitalization and momentum (BEM Table 11.5)
#| echo: false

show_table(pl.DataFrame([
    row for weight in weights
    for row in two_way_results(size_momentum, weight, quintiles, show_cells=True)
]))
```

### Momentum Among Small Stocks

Restrict the first sort to the bottom fifth of the capitalization distribution.
Split that group into four portfolios and sort each portfolio into `mom` quintiles.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem11-small
#| tbl-cap: Dependent momentum sorts within the smallest capitalization quintile (BEM Table 11.6)

small = sort_panel.filter(pl.col("cap") <= pl.col("cap").quantile(0.20).over("month"))
small = assign_portfolio(small, "cap", 4, "month", label="control")
small = assign_portfolio(small, "mom", 5, ["month", "control"], label="target")
small_momentum = portfolio_months(small.drop_nulls("target"), ["control", "target"])

show_table(pl.DataFrame([
    row for weight in weights
    for row in two_way_results(
        small_momentum, weight, ["0–5%", "5–10%", "10–15%", "15–20%"],
        show_cells=True, show_average=False,
    )
]))
```

### Controlling for Beta and Book-to-Market

The dependent sorts calculate `mom` breakpoints within each beta or `bm` quintile.
The independent sorts use the intersection of two sets of breakpoints computed separately across stocks for each variable.
The tables show the high-minus-low `mom` spread within each control quintile and its average across the control quintiles.

```{python}
sort_variables = {"beta": "Beta", "cap": "Market cap", "bm": "`bm`"}


def two_way_spreads(pairs, *, dependent, momentum_first=False):
    rows = []
    for control, target in pairs:
        monthly = bivariate_months(sort_panel, control, target, nyse=False, dependent=dependent)
        omit = {"cap": "smb", "bm": "hml"}.get(target)
        ff_factors = [factor for factor in ff3 if factor != omit]
        characteristic = target if momentum_first else control
        for weight in weights:
            rows.extend(
                {"Characteristic": sort_variables[characteristic], **row}
                for row in two_way_results(monthly, weight, quintiles, ff_factors=ff_factors)
            )
    return pl.DataFrame(rows)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem11-dependent
#| tbl-cap: Momentum spreads from dependent sorts controlling for beta or book-to-market (BEM Table 11.7)
#| echo: false

show_table(two_way_spreads([("beta", "mom"), ("bm", "mom")], dependent=True))
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem11-independent
#| tbl-cap: Momentum spreads from independent sorts controlling for beta, capitalization, or book-to-market (BEM Table 11.8)
#| echo: false

show_table(two_way_spreads([(control, "mom") for control in sort_variables], dependent=False))
```

### Controlling for Momentum

Reverse the sort order to ask whether differences associated with beta, capitalization, or `bm` remain within `mom` quintiles.
For Table 11.9, we follow BEM's discussion and calculate the second set of breakpoints within each `mom` quintile.
For capitalization spreads, omit `smb` from the FF regression.
For `bm` spreads, omit `hml`.

show_table(two_way_spreads(reverse_pairs, dependent=True, momentum_first=True))

### Fama–MacBeth Regressions

Regress next month's excess return on `mom` and combinations of beta, log capitalization, and `bm`.
Winsorize the regressors at 0.5% in each tail within each month.
Report the average monthly coefficients and estimate their standard errors using six Newey–West lags.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem11-fama-macbeth
#| tbl-cap: Monthly Fama–MacBeth regressions of next-month excess returns (BEM Table 11.11)

from itertools import combinations

from eap_pl import fama_macbeth_table

terms = {"mom": "`mom`", **controls}
specifications = [
    ["mom", *subset]
    for n in range(len(controls) + 1)
    for subset in combinations(controls, n)
]
show_table(fama_macbeth_table(panel, specifications, terms, digits=3))
```

In the full specification, a 100-percentage-point difference in `mom` corresponds to about 0.70 percentage points in next month's fitted excess return.

## The Momentum Factor

The [Kenneth French Data Library](https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/Ken.French/Data_Library/det_mom_factor.html) constructs its momentum factor using six value-weighted portfolios formed on size and prior return.
The sorts use an NYSE median for size and NYSE 30th and 70th percentiles for prior return.
The factor averages the returns of the small- and large-stock winner portfolios and subtracts the average return of the corresponding loser portfolios.
We use the December 2024 release listed in the book's setup instructions and plot January 1927 through December 2012, the period in BEM.

```{python}
#| label: fig-bem11-mom
#| fig-cap: Compounded and cumulative log returns of the momentum factor, January 1927–December 2012 (BEM Figure 11.1)

from io import StringIO
from pathlib import Path
import re

from eap_pl import plot_cumulative_returns

archive = Path("data/momentum-202412.csv").read_text()
monthly_rows = re.findall(r"(?m)^\s*(\d{6},[^\r\n]+)", archive)
momentum_factor = (
    pl.read_csv(
        StringIO("\n".join(monthly_rows)), has_header=False, new_columns=["ym", "mom"],
        schema_overrides={"mom": pl.String},
    )
    .filter(pl.col("ym").is_between(192701, 201212))
    .select(
        date=(pl.col("ym").cast(pl.String) + "01").str.to_date("%Y%m%d"),
        mom=pl.col("mom").str.strip_chars().cast(pl.Float64) / 100,
    )
    .sort("date")
    .with_columns(
        compounded=(1 + pl.col("mom")).cum_prod() - 1,
        cumulative_log=pl.col("mom").log1p().cum_sum(),
    )
)
assert momentum_factor.height == 1032
assert momentum_factor.select(pl.col("mom").is_finite().all()).item()
plot_cumulative_returns(momentum_factor, y_label="Cumulative momentum factor return")
```

The compounded series shows a sharp drawdown in 2009.

## The Fama–French–Carhart Four-Factor Model

@carhart1997 adds a momentum factor to the three stock-market factors of @famaFrench1993.
The four-factor model is BEM's Equation (11.2).

$$
r_{p,t}=\alpha_p+\beta_{\mathrm{MKT},p}\mathrm{MKT}_t
+\beta_{\mathrm{SMB},p}\mathrm{SMB}_t+\beta_{\mathrm{HML},p}\mathrm{HML}_t
+\beta_{\mathrm{MOM},p}\mathrm{MOM}_t+\varepsilon_{p,t}.
$$ {#eq-bem11-ffc}

Here $r_{p,t}$ is the excess return of portfolio $p$, and $\alpha_p$ is the intercept after accounting for its exposures to the market, size, value, and momentum factors.
